reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme of the purine salvage pathway
Loss of salvage diverts adenine to oxidation by xanthine oxidase, producing the highly insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (2,8-DHA)
2,8-DHA precipitates as radiolucent urinary stones and as intratubular crystals, causing renal colic, haematuria, recurrent stones and crystal nephropathy
It is a major under-recognised cause of chronic kidney disease and can present with graft dysfunction after kidney transplantation if undiagnosed
2,8-DHA stones are radiolucent and can be mistaken for uric acid stones, but unlike uric acid they do not dissolve with urinary alkalinisation
Diagnosis rests on identifying 2,8-DHA in stone or crystal analysis (round brown crystals on urine microscopy), enzyme assay or APRT gene testing
Management is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor to block 2,8-DHA formation, together with high fluid intake and dietary purine moderation; urinary alkalinisation does not help
reference.pathophysiology: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase normally salvages free adenine by combining it with phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate to form adenosine monophosphate. When the enzyme is deficient, adenine cannot be recycled and is instead oxidised by xanthine oxidase, first to 8-hydroxyadenine and then to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine. This end product is extremely insoluble across the physiological urinary pH range, so it crystallises within the renal tubules and urinary tract, producing stones and progressive crystalline tubulointerstitial damage. Because the enzyme block lies upstream, inhibiting xanthine oxidase effectively prevents 2,8-DHA generation.
additionalDifferentials: Uric acid urolithiasis (also radiolucent but pH-responsive)
Hereditary xanthinuria and other radiolucent stone disorders
Other crystalline nephropathies (e.g. oxalate, drug crystals)
Idiopathic chronic kidney disease of unknown cause
additionalInvestigations: Stone analysis and urine microscopy for characteristic 2,8-DHA crystals
Infrared spectroscopy or capillary electrophoresis to confirm 2,8-DHA composition
Molecular genetic testing of the APRT gene
Renal function and urinalysis to assess crystal nephropathy
Renal tract imaging for radiolucent calculi
redFlags: Progressive or unexplained chronic kidney disease, especially with crystals on biopsy
Acute kidney injury from crystal obstruction
Early graft dysfunction after renal transplantation from recurrent crystal deposition
Recurrent stone disease from infancy or childhood
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and continuous xanthine oxidase inhibitor therapy the prognosis is excellent and renal function can be preserved; delayed diagnosis may lead to irreversible chronic kidney disease or loss of a transplanted kidney.
pitfalls: Misclassifying 2,8-DHA stones as uric acid stones and prescribing ineffective alkalinisation
Failing to diagnose the condition before kidney transplantation, risking rapid graft injury
Overlooking crystalline nephropathy as a cause of unexplained chronic kidney disease
Not maintaining lifelong therapy, as crystal formation resumes if treatment stops
Missing the diagnosis in adults because it can present at any age
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
